demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette: Three years ago, Arjun was deep in the west wing of a client's historic townhouse. He had positioned a stepladder to reach the top of a tall linen closet. The floor was newly waxed, slick under his work boots. When he shifted his weight to grab a heavy cast-iron ironing board leaning against the wall, the ladder's rubber feet caught on a hairline crack in the tile. It buckled. The board slipped from his grip, pivoted on the edge of the step, and fell backward. It struck the homeowner's nephew, who had just walked into the hall, squarely across the temple. There was no slow-motion unraveling, just two sharp frames that lock in his mind: the sudden tilt of the ladder beneath his boots, and the sickening arc of the iron board descending toward the man's face. The event happened because of the way he had acted; he was certain of that. The aftermath did not bring a steady stream of recollection but a series of frozen moments that would drop into his awareness without warning. Sometimes it was the smell of lemon floor polish on a Tuesday morning; other times, it was the particular squeak of a metal hinge or the sight of a heavy object balanced on a high surface. In those moments, the hallway would warp, his palms would sweat, and the two pictures would snap back into place so completely that his breath would catch. When the image returned, a hot, sharp fury would coil in his chest. It was not directed at the man who had been hurt. The anger was aimed at himself, at the way his hands had moved, at the carelessness that felt so alien to the man who had always prided himself on quiet competence. What frightened him most was how instantly the room would fill with the memory, leaving no space for anything else. His job as a residential cleaner had required steady hands and a meticulous eye for three decades. After the incident, Arjun found himself avoiding the very tasks that once came naturally. He began taking the long route to the east staircase of each new house, refusing to use stepladders, and he started cleaning each room in a slow, almost halting pace. He quit the agency that employed him at the historic properties, taking lower-paying jobs in single-story homes where the ceiling felt closer and the corners offered fewer places for things to fall. The change accumulated quietly. He stopped answering calls from old friends who asked if he wanted to help them move or do minor renovations. He began spending his days in his small, dim apartment in Queens, drawn to the silence because movement reminded him of the shift in weight, the crack in the tile, the sudden arc. Over time, Arjun had come to believe he was fundamentally reckless, a trait he had spent his life fighting against. At the same time, nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. His days and nights ran side by side without crossing, each occupying its own space in his mind. He stopped volunteering at the community center he had attended for years, stopped tending to the small balcony garden that had always given him structure. The work that once grounded him now felt like an exercise in waiting. He could not reconcile the man he was with the man who had caused harm, and the disconnect made his days feel weightless. He carried both convictions forward, parallel and unyielding. Arjun finally walked into the clinic after a regular shift at a corporate office. He was wiping down a supply closet shelf when a heavy binder slipped from a neighbor's grip and landed on the rubber floor with a dull thud. The sound had paralyzed him against the wall, his heart hammering against his ribs, the two frames flashing behind his eyes until he had to leave before the shift ended. He had spent his life believing he could manage a space with careful work, but he no longer trusted his own hands or his own judgment. He came to the appointment hoping for something he could not name-perhaps a way to quiet the fury that rose in him when he remembered, or a way to stop feeling like a stranger in his own routine. He did not know if he would ever feel purposeful again, but he knew he could no longer carry the weight of the mistake alone.
